## Where session 1 left off

Session 1 built the vocabulary. Today is about patterns.

- Patterns are (comparatively) easy
- Recognizing which problems fit a pattern is harder
- So: a few design principles first, then look at actual code

::: {.notes}
Handoff from Jackson, thirty seconds. Be honest that this is a detour. The groundwork
worth laying is a few principles, not a catalogue of patterns. Flag that the second half
is `stitch-etl` Alberta so nobody is waiting for a pattern list that never comes.
:::

---

# Design background

---

## ETL systems are just software {data-topic="Design background"}

Nothing about a pipeline makes it a different kind of software.

- Typical "users" are other systems, or us: developers and admins
- Fewer user-facing constraints than a GUI or a web app, but no special ones
- Everything that applies to designing software applies here

::: {.notes}
Say it plainly and move on. The point is permission to use ordinary design thinking rather
than hunting for ETL-specific rules.
:::

---

## "Design" vs "Architecture" {data-topic="Design background"}

Treat them as the same thing today.

- The distinction is real, but it's a topic for another session
- I don't think anything I've seen at SPD warrants it
- I'll try to be consistent. Don't get hung up on which word I use

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds. Saying this once buys the rest of the hour without someone stopping to
argue the terminology.
:::

---

## What is design? {data-topic="Design background"}

> The decisions and elements that determine how software satisfies its
> requirements within its constraints.

Usually covers:

- Components, and what each one is responsible for
- Their interfaces and relationships
- Algorithms and data representations
- Policies for how the system runs and how it can change

::: {.notes}
The definition is broad on purpose. Don't read the bullets out. Pick two and give an ETL
example of each.
:::

---

## What design is not {data-topic="Design background"}

- Diagrams and docs
- Technology choices: framework, library, database engine
- "Service oriented" or microservices
- Cloud resources and infrastructure
- Specific abstractions or patterns

Any of these can express or support a design. None of them are one.

::: {.notes}
Fast slide. The list matters more than any single item on it. Expect pushback on
microservices, and give that one about ten seconds.
:::

---

## Every system has an architecture {data-topic="Design background"}

Whether anyone intended one or not.

- It's recursive: every component has its own
- A system can follow very different principles than its parts
- You can reason about one component without holding the whole system in your head

::: {.notes}
The recursive part is what makes the rest of the session usable. Nobody has to redesign a
system to apply any of this to a single module.
:::

---

## Running code, not documents {data-topic="Design background"}

Design is embodied by what actually runs, not by the files or the docs.

- Written descriptions drift from the system, and code drifts from what's deployed
- Worth thinking about how objects and processes behave at runtime, not only how
  modules are arranged
- Also why application architecture and deployment architecture are separate questions

::: {.notes}
This one landed late while I was preparing, and it matters more than it looks.

Title replaces "The design is what runs". Alternatives if this one doesn't land:
"Where the design actually exists", or "Documentation drifts".
:::

---

## Design is hard {data-topic="Design background"}

- Mostly cost/benefit analysis, and not a precise one
- Which trade-offs fit the requirements you actually have?
- You get better at it by doing it, and by getting it wrong
- AI still can't do it consistently. It needs the mushy meat parts

::: {.callout-tip title="Opting out is still a choice"}
Deciding not to think about design is a design decision. You just make it by default.
:::

::: {.notes}
Last framing slide. The callout is the thing to land before the principles start.
:::

---

# Idempotency

---

## What it means {data-topic="Idempotency"}

::: {.notes}
Sharpen it past session 1: calling something many times leaves system state the same as
calling it once. It says nothing about the return value. The second half is the part people
get wrong.
:::

---

## !!!

::: {.callout-warning title="Devil in the (implementation) details"}
- Assymetry between user/caller expectations and implementation
- No real enforcement of guarantees
- A `GET` handler can write to the database on every request
- A `__setitem__` can append to a list every time you assign the same key.
```python
 class MyClass:
     def __setitem__(self, key, val):
          self._keys.append(key)
          self._data_dict[key] = val
```
Be aware of conventions as misalignment can negatively impact usability.
:::

::: {.notes}
Idempotency is a convention that callers design against, and nothing stops you from
breaking it. Facetious tone here. Needs the `__setitem__` code block.
:::

---

## Familiar examples {data-topic="Idempotency"}

::: {.notes}
Idempotent: `set.add`, `dict.update`, `min`/`max`, HTTP `GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE`, Bicep and
Terraform. Not: `list.append`, `POST`, `PATCH`, and most functions you write. Aim for
recognition rather than definitions. Code block of short Python examples.
:::

---

## In SQL {data-topic="Idempotency"}

::: {.notes}
Idempotent without effort: `SELECT`, and `UPDATE`/`DELETE` with a `WHERE`. Bought with
syntax: `CREATE OR REPLACE`, `IF NOT EXISTS`, `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`.
Most directly useful slide in the section for this audience. Needs a SQL block.
:::

---

## Effect on calling code {data-topic="Idempotency"}

::: {.notes}
A guarantee at the boundary removes branching from every caller. Walk the non-idempotent
`save_names` first so the cleanup loop in the caller is visible, then the idempotent
version where that loop disappears. Complexity moved, it didn't vanish.

Needs both `save_names` blocks from the script, side by side if they fit.
:::

---

## Trade-offs {data-topic="Idempotency"}

::: {.notes}
Usually harder to implement. Weigh the extra effort against what downstream components can
absorb. For anything bigger than a single script, lean toward it.
:::

---

# Information hiding

---

## What it means {data-topic="Information hiding"}

::: {.notes}
Keeping implementation decisions private from other components. Central idea of the
session. It narrows what you have to hold in your head while designing, which is most of
the value.
:::

---

## Delaying decisions {data-topic="Information hiding"}

::: {.notes}
If a design keeps a choice reversible, you decide later with more information. Database
schemas are hard to change, so hiding the schema behind an interface buys time to learn
more before committing.
:::

---

## `persistence.py` {data-topic="Information hiding"}

::: {.notes}
Stub the interface other components call: `get_user()`, `query_landfills()`,
`upsert_reservoir_data()`. Callers don't depend on how data is stored. CSVs now, Postgres
later, without touching anything upstream. Needs the stub module as a code block.
:::

---

## External data providers {data-topic="Information hiding"}

::: {.notes}
`GEMExtractionClient`, `CCReservoirsAPI`. When a provider changes its response format,
auth, or rate limiting, exactly one module changes.
:::

---

## Trade-offs {data-topic="Information hiding"}

::: {.notes}
Mostly attention during design, and compartmentalizing is awkward at first. Of the four,
this has the fewest trade-offs and the widest use, especially while refactoring.
:::

---

# Single responsibility

---

## What it means {data-topic="Single responsibility"}

> Gather together the things that change for the same reasons.
> Separate things that change for different reasons.

::: {.notes}
A guide for grouping capabilities, not a rule about size. Close to information hiding: the
decisions you hide are usually the reasons something changes.
:::

---

## Not "do one thing" {data-topic="Single responsibility"}

::: {.notes}
The common misreading. "A function should do one thing" and the Unix philosophy are
different claims. Reason for change is the grouping criterion, not count of operations.
:::

---

## Splitting `persistence.py` {data-topic="Single responsibility"}

::: {.notes}
Reuse the earlier example. It starts as one module. It splits when file access and database
access begin changing for different reasons, not because it got long. Needs before/after
code blocks.
:::

---

## Modules and packages {data-topic="Single responsibility"}

::: {.notes}
Python modules and packages already give you boundaries to examine. Adherence is a
direction, not a gate: look at what changed together over the last year to decide whether
something should split.
:::

---

## Trade-offs {data-topic="Single responsibility"}

::: {.notes}
More subjective than the others and more dependent on domain and on a component's
relationships. Hardest of the four to argue about productively in review.
:::

---

# Dependency inversion

---

## What it means {data-topic="Dependency inversion"}

::: {.notes}
Depend on abstractions that rarely change. A `Protocol` carries no implementation details
at all. Keep this short and let the examples carry it.
:::

---

## Provider schemas in core logic {data-topic="Dependency inversion"}

::: {.callout-warning title="A common way this goes wrong"}
An external API's field names and types show up in the module holding your business rules.
Core logic now depends on a decision made outside the organization.
:::

::: {.notes}
The failure the whole session circles, and the one most likely to be sitting in a repo
someone in the room owns.
:::

---

## Dependencies and control flow {data-topic="Dependency inversion"}

::: {.notes}
Control flow often dictates a dependency: A depends on B so it can create one and call its
methods. When B is more abstract than A, nothing needs inverting. You invert by inserting
an interface when A is the higher level component, which shows up most on writes and
responses, where data flows outward. They are not always opposed.
:::

---

## Orchestrating with interfaces {data-topic="Dependency inversion"}

::: {.notes}
The orchestrator depends on interfaces rather than concrete classes. Show two extract
client implementations against one interface, and one implementation for the others.
Idempotent implementations mean the orchestrator carries less retry and error handling.
Needs a code block.
:::

---

## Inverting a dependency {data-topic="Dependency inversion"}

::: {.notes}
Before: the high level component depends on the input handler. After: the high level
component declares the interface, and the dependency points from the low level component
inward. Needs before/after code blocks.
:::

---

## Trade-offs {data-topic="Dependency inversion"}

::: {.notes}
Code volume and indirection. The one principle here that's easy to overshoot, so say that
rather than selling it.
:::

---

# Wrapping up

---

## What to take away {data-topic="Wrapping up"}

> Before you implement or change a component, decide how callers should use it,
> what they must be able to assume, and what they should be insulated from.

::: {.notes}
Tie back to the opening: this contains changes, makes results verifiable, and makes an
unfamiliar repo navigable. On a small team, recognizing the same boundaries and guarantees
across projects is what lets us move between each other's work.
:::
